articles.title: From Tutorial Consumer to Operator: The Skills Gap CMD Master Targets
articles.excerpt: Watching CLI tutorials feels like progress. You nod at PATH diagrams. You pause a video to copy a command. You finish a playlist titled “Windows Command Line Full Course.” Then a production incident h…
articles.body: Watching CLI tutorials feels like progress. You nod at PATH diagrams. You pause a video to copy a command. You finish a playlist titled “Windows Command Line Full Course.” Then a production incident hands you a blank prompt and the playlist doesn’t play in your head. That gap— tutorial consumer → operator —is the product problem I’m building around with CMD Master. What tutorial consumption trains Recognition of concepts when cued. Happy-path sequences in the author’s order. Confidence that is bound to narration. What operators need Initiation without a narrator. State awareness (cwd, env, shell identity). Recovery from errors under mild stress. Transfer across CMD, PowerShell, and sometimes Bash contracts on one OS. Those are different muscles. Screenshots and lectures can support them.

articles.title: From 100 Million Events to 1,200 Pixels: Engineering a Data-Heavy Dashboard
articles.excerpt: Your dashboard has a chart that is about 1,200 pixels wide. Behind it sits a table that grows by a few million rows a day. Somebody opens the page, picks "last 30 days", and expects to see request vol…
articles.body: Your dashboard has a chart that is about 1,200 pixels wide. Behind it sits a table that grows by a few million rows a day. Somebody opens the page, picks "last 30 days", and expects to see request volume, cost, error rate and p95 latency — immediately, and again a second later when they drag across a spike to zoom in. Somewhere between those two facts — millions of rows on one side, a few hundred visible values on the other — your architecture decides where the data gets smaller. Usually nobody makes that decision on purpose. It happens in the first version of the API, and it stays there until the dashboard gets slow. This article is about making that decision deliberately.
articles.author: Sergey

articles.title: A 2B vision model judged my listing photos. It knew what was wrong and still could not tell me whether to ship them.
articles.excerpt: Day 288 of DailyBuild. Today's build is Photo Gate: one photo in, five typed decisions out, in a single forward pass, on my laptop, with no API key and no tokens generated. I gave it a job I actually…
articles.body: Day 288 of DailyBuild . Today's build is Photo Gate: one photo in, five typed decisions out, in a single forward pass, on my laptop, with no API key and no tokens generated. I gave it a job I actually care about. Would this photo get a click on a second hand marketplace, or does the seller need to go take another one? What a decision model is You send a state, which here is an image plus a short line of context. You send questions with lettered options. The model reads the option letter logits at each answer slot in one forward pass and returns a probability for every option. It does not write a sentence. It cannot invent an answer outside the options you gave it. That is the whole idea of the class. Jev and the twenty alternatives that shipped after it are all built on it.

articles.body: Getting an enforcement email from Google Play — a rejection, a suspension, a strike — triggers panic. Most developers fire off an angry, vague appeal within minutes, or give up entirely. Both are mistakes. A Google Play appeal is not a customer support ticket. It's a structured policy argument reviewed against a specific policy clause. The difference between appeals that succeed and those that fail comes down to preparation, specificity, and evidence. Here's the playbook. Step 1: Understand Exactly What Happened Before writing a single word, decode the enforcement notice.

articles.title: Did a giant object collide with Earth to form the moon?
articles.excerpt: Known as the giant-impact hypothesis, this proposed event involves a collision between Earth and a hypothetical Mars-sized protoplanet astronomers call Theia.
articles.body: For as long as humans have watched the night sky, we have wondered about the moon , pondering everything from its alien appearance to its influence over phenomena on Earth such as ocean tides, climate stability, and even the natural rhythms of many organisms. Among the many questions we have about Earth's lone natural satellite, one remains preeminent: what are the moon's origins , and how long has it orbited Earth? Today, the leading theory among astronomers is that deep in our planet's past — perhaps within roughly the first 100 million years of solar system history — Earth collided with a planet-sized object, creating the moon within a period that may have been as short as just a few hours .

articles.body: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. articles.title: Returning the first samples from a Martian moon: Inside the science of Japan's bold MMX mission to Mars
articles.excerpt: Japan's mission to Mars' moons could answer a decades old question dividing the origins of Phobos and Deimos between two conflicting theories, and make history as the first spacecraft to return to Ear…
articles.body: Japan's mission to Mars is one of the most ambitious in spaceflight history. It aims to become the first spacecraft to return to Earth from Mars orbit, carrying with it the first-ever samples from the Red Planet system. The mission, known as Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), is a first-of-its-kind endeavor to study the origin of Mars' moons Phobos and Deimos. The robust undertaking includes a landing on Phobos to collect the samples — which will likely be the first from the Mars system to return to Earth — and a search for evidence that could shed light on events during the formation of the solar system billions of years ago. articles.title: Computer scientist Margaret Hamilton was a problem-solver for the ages (op-ed)
articles.excerpt: The world will miss Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering programmer who helped NASA land Apollo astronauts on the moon. But we will always have her example to inspire us.
articles.body: Dean Robbins is a journalist and children's author. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights . The pioneering computer scientist Margaret Hamilton , who died on Sept. 30 at age 90, played a key role in putting astronauts on the moon. She was a problem-solver extraordinaire, and it all started in early childhood. Considering the name "daddy longlegs" unfair to female arachnids, young Margaret decided to call half of them "mommy longlegs." Wondering why the neighborhood baseball players were all boys, she determined to join the team herself. As she grew up in the 1940s and '50s, Margaret noticed a similar problem with various professions. Why were doctors, judges and scientists almost always men?

articles.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
articles.excerpt: The actions could have resulted in criminal charges had humans been behind the keyboard.
articles.body: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own.
